title: Dictionary Order & Alphabet
summary: Arranging words as in a dictionary, alphabet-position arithmetic (EJOTY anchors, from-right = 27 − p, shifts), modified-alphabet sequences, and the dictionary rank of a word among its letter arrangements. The whole topic runs on one rule — the first differing letter decides, and a prefix comes before its extensions — plus small, careful counting on paper.

subtopics.title: Dictionary order rules
subtopics.concept:
Words sort letter by letter from the left. At the first position where two words differ, the word with the earlier alphabet comes first — everything after that position is irrelevant. Two refinements decide the tricky cases:

1. **Prefix rule**: if one word runs out of letters while matching the other (SCAN vs SCANTY), the **shorter word comes first** — an ending acts like a space, and a space precedes every letter. (But SCANDAL vs SCANTY is settled at the 5th letter: D < T, so SCANDAL < SCANTY.)
2. **No skipping**: compare position by position; a later difference never overrides an earlier one.

Method for 5-word arrangements: build the words' common prefixes on paper, sort group by group, then read off the asked slot (first / middle / last).

tricks.title: Find the first split point
tricks.body: Write the words one under another and slide a finger left to right until the letters first differ. That single column decides the entire comparison — ignore all later letters.

example.q:
**Q.** Order: SIGN, SIGHT, SIGNAL.

**Sol.** All start SIG. 4th letters: N, H, N → SIGHT (H) before the rest; SIGN vs SIGNAL: SIGN is a prefix → SIGN first. Order: SIGHT, SIGN, SIGNAL.
example.solution: The first differing letter settles everything; prefix pairs end shortest-first.

mistakes: Judging words by length instead of first-difference.
Putting SCANDAL after SCANTY because 'scanty feels later' — compare D vs T.
Forgetting the prefix rule: the shorter of two prefix words leads.
subtopics.notes:
### One rule runs the whole topic

A real dictionary sorts words letter by letter from the left, and so does every question in this topic. At the **first position where two words differ**, the word with the **earlier letter** comes first. That single rule answers every arrangement question — the skill is applying it without getting lost.

**The comparison algorithm.** To order any group of words:
1. Compare the first letters. Words sort into groups by their first letter: all A-words before all B-words, and so on.
2. Inside a group, compare the second letters; then the third; keep going until the words separate.
3. If one word runs out of letters while matching the other word letter for letter (Cart vs Carton), the **shorter word comes first** — it is a prefix of the longer one.

Work with paper, not memory: stack the words vertically so the columns line up, then scan column by column. The first column that is not identical splits the group into sub-groups; recurse inside each sub-group.

**Two classic traps.**
- *The later-letter trap:* early matches lull you into relaxing. Scant, Scan, Scandal all share S-C-A-N; the decision hides at the fifth letter (t vs nothing vs d). Stay letter-by-letter to the very end.
- *The prefix trap:* a shorter word that matches a longer one's start always comes **before** it — Scan before Scant, Play before Player. Options routinely offer the reverse because it 'feels' longer-word-first.

**Words with same letters, different order.** Angel vs Angle: identical multiset of letters, but the third letter (e vs n) splits them — Angel first. The rule never changes: first differing position, earlier letter wins.

**Reading the question direction.** "Which comes first / last", "which is third", "which pair is adjacent", "which comes just after X" — all four are the same sort followed by a different lookup. Do the full sort once, number the slots 1-2-3-4-5, and answer any of these variants from the numbered list.

### Quick revision
- Sort letter by letter from the left; the first differing letter decides.
- A shorter word that is a prefix of a longer one comes first (Scan → Scant → Scandal).
- Stack words vertically and scan columns — never juggle in your head.
- Same letters, different order: the first differing position still decides (Angel before Angle).
- Sort once, number the slots, then answer 'first / last / third / adjacent' from the list.

**Where marks are actually lost.** Almost never in the rule — always in execution: a misread letter pair (m/n, r/s), a forgotten prefix, or answering 'first' when the question asked 'last'. The numbered-line habit kills all three: order on paper, read the slot, and reread the question's direction word (first / last / second / middle) before marking.

patterns.name: First differing letter decides
patterns.howToSpot: Two or three words sharing an opening; the question asks which comes first or last.
patterns.logic:
1. Scan letter by letter to the first position where the words differ.
2. The earlier letter at that position wins the earlier slot.
3. Ignore how long the shared part is — only the first difference matters.

*Why it works:* dictionary order is exactly lexicographic order on the left-most difference.

example.q: **Which comes first in the dictionary: Market, Margin or Marble?**
example.solution: All share MAR; 4th letters k / g / b → b earliest → **Marble** comes first.

patterns.name: Shorter prefix sorts first
patterns.howToSpot: One word is exactly the start of another (Sand, Sandwich) — a prefix pair.
patterns.logic:
1. If word A matches word B letter for letter and A has no letters left, A is B's prefix.
2. The prefix comes **before** the longer word.
3. Among several extensions, compare the letter right after the stem.

*Why it works:* a dictionary cannot fit anything between a word and itself, so the short form lists first.

example.q: **Which of these comes first: Sand, Sandy, Sandwich or Sandal?**
example.solution: Sand is a prefix of the other three → **Sand** comes first.

patterns.name: Deep ties beyond the third letter
patterns.howToSpot: 4-6 words sharing a long stem where the decision hides at the 4th-6th letter.
patterns.logic:
1. Strip the common stem and write only the tails.
2. Sort tails letter by letter; the earliest tail letter takes the earliest slot.
3. Prefix tails (empty tail) sort first inside their group.

*Why it works:* the comparison rule does not care how deep the difference hides.

example.q: **Arrange Sure, Surge, Surgeon, Surplus, Surreal. Which comes third?**
example.solution: 4th letters: e / g / g / p / r → Sure, Surge, Surgeon, Surplus, Surreal → third = **Surgeon**.

patterns.name: Slot lookups: middle and adjacent pairs
patterns.howToSpot: After sorting, the question asks for the middle word or an adjacent pair rather than first/last.
patterns.logic:
1. Produce the full numbered order first — never answer adjacent questions by instinct.
2. Middle of 5 words = slot 3; of 4 words, slots 2 and 3 share the middle.
3. Adjacent = slot numbers differing by exactly 1.

*Why it works:* every lookup variant reads off the same sorted list.

example.q: **Arrange Melon, Melody, Mellow, Member. Which two are adjacent in the dictionary?**
example.solution: 4th letters: b / l / l / o → Member, Mellow, Melody, Melon. Adjacent pair: **Melon and Melody**.

subtopics.title: Arranging words and picking slots
subtopics.concept:
Standard question: 4-6 words are given; arrange them as in a dictionary and answer which comes first, second, middle, or last. Practical pipeline:

1. Group words by their first letter (usually all share one or two letters).
2. Inside a group, repeat by the second letter, then the third — the groups shrink fast.
3. Count down to the asked slot: 'third from the left' = the third word in the final order.

Answer options are usually the words themselves; wrong options come from comparing at the wrong position — which is exactly what the split-point method prevents.

tricks.title: Slot-count from the left
tricks.body: Once sorted, number the words 1, 2, 3… and simply read the asked position. 'Comes last' = highest position; 'middle of five' = position 3.

example.q:
**Q.** Cable, Cabin, Cabaret, Cabbage — which comes third?

**Sol.** CABA < CABB < CABI < CABL → Cabaret, Cabbage, Cabin, Cable → third = **Cabin**.
example.solution: Sort once, count to the slot; never re-compare for each option.

mistakes: Re-sorting mentally for every option instead of fixing one order.
Answering 'third from the right' with the third word from the left.
subtopics.notes:
### The standard 4-6 word arrangement

This is the topic's workhorse: a list of 4-6 similar words, and one lookup — "which comes third", "which is last", "which comes just after X", "which is second from the right". The method never changes; only the lookup does.

**Step 1 — group by the shared stem.** Exam words almost always share a long prefix (Stat-, Colon-, Dec-). Find the stem and draw it once; only the letters **after** the stem matter. Statue, Status, Statute, Stature, Station all share STAT — the fight starts at the fifth letter.

**Step 2 — split at the first difference.** Line up the words, ignore the common stem, and look at the next letter of each. Sort by those letters. Ties inside a letter move one position deeper. In the STAT family: Station (i) separates immediately; Statue/Status/Statute/Stature all show E/S/E/R at position six, then sort by the seventh where needed.

**Step 3 — apply the prefix rule inside ties.** When one word is a stem-with-nothing (Colon inside Colonial... but also Decamp family: Decay vs December), remember: exact prefix sorts before its extensions; among extensions, the next letter decides.

**Step 4 — number and read.** Write the final order as a numbered line, 1 to N, then answer whatever was asked:
- "Third word" → slot 3.
- "Second from the right" → slot N−1.
- "Just after X" → slot of X plus one.
- "Adjacent pair" → two words whose slot numbers differ by exactly 1.

**Speed practice pays twice.** These questions are pure procedure — the same 30-second routine solves every one. Errors come almost only from mis-comparing one letter pair (mixing up m/n order, reading r before s) or from mis-counting slots ('second from right' vs 'second'). Both are prevented by the numbered line: letters decide the order, numbers decide the answer.

**Check with extremes.** Before locking an answer, confirm the obvious: the word with the alphabetically earliest deep letter should sit near the left end, the latest near the right end. If your final order violates that instinct, re-scan column two — a transposed pair is the usual cause.

### Quick revision
- Strip the shared stem; the battle starts at the first letter after it.
- Prefix (bare stem) sorts before any extension of itself.
- Write the full numbered order, then read the requested slot off it.
- 'Second from the right' = slot N−1; 'just after X' = X's slot + 1.
- Sanity-check: earliest deciding letter at the left end, latest at the right.

**Time target.** A practiced 5-word arrangement takes 30-40 seconds: 5 for the stem, 15 for the column scan, 10 for the numbered line, 5 for the lookup. If you are past a minute, you are re-sorting in your head — restart on paper; it is faster than a third mental pass.

patterns.name: Arrange and pick the slot
patterns.howToSpot: 4-6 words; 'which is the Nth word in dictionary order' (from the left).
patterns.logic:
1. Strip the shared stem; sort by the first differing tail letter.
2. Write the numbered order 1..N.
3. Read slot N and check it against the extreme words.

*Why it works:* one sort, then a positional lookup.

example.q: **Arrange Chalk, Charm, Chart, Chase, Chatter. Which is the fourth word?**
example.solution: 4th letters: l / r / r / s / t → Chalk, Charm, Chart, Chase, Chatter → fourth = **Chase**.

patterns.name: Prefix vs later-letter battle
patterns.howToSpot: The list mixes a bare stem with extensions that fight over a later letter.
patterns.logic:
1. The bare stem sorts before all extensions.
2. Extensions sort by the letter right after the stem; ties go one letter deeper.
3. Re-scan the deciding column twice — one misread flips two slots.

*Why it works:* first difference decides, at whatever depth it hides.

example.q: **Arrange Mystery, Mystic, Myself, Myopia. Which comes first?**
example.solution: 3rd letters: s / s / s / o → Myopia first; among the s-words, 4th letters e/t/t → Myself, then Mystery (5th e) before Mystic (5th i). First = **Myopia**.

patterns.name: Extremes and immediate neighbours
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which comes last / just after X / immediately before Y' — neighbour lookups on the sorted list.
patterns.logic:
1. Sort fully and number the slots.
2. 'Just after X' = X's slot + 1; 'immediately before Y' = Y's slot − 1.
3. For 'last', only the deepest group's final word matters.

*Why it works:* neighbours are slot arithmetic on the finished order.

example.q: **Which comes just after Colony: Colonel, Colony, Column, Colour, Colossus?**
example.solution: Order: Colonel, Colony, Colossus, Colour, Column → just after Colony = **Colossus**.

patterns.name: Counting from the right end
patterns.howToSpot: 'Second from the right', 'third from the end' — the slot is counted from the back.
patterns.logic:
1. Sort and number 1..N as usual.
2. k-th from the right = slot N + 1 − k.
3. Convert first, then read — do not count backwards on the raw list.

*Why it works:* mirror of the slot lookup: the right end is slot N.

example.q: **Arrange Judge, Judo, Joust, Journal, Jostle. Which word is second from the right?**
example.solution: Order: Jostle, Journal, Joust, Judge, Judo → slot 5 + 1 − 2 = 4 → **Judge**.

subtopics.title: Letter positions and shifts
subtopics.concept:
Memorise the anchor word **EJOTY**: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25. Every position question becomes a small shift:

- Letter at position p: read off from EJOTY, adjust by the difference.
- p-th from the right: position = 27 − p from the left.
- k letters to the right of position p: p + k; to the left: p − k (stay inside 1–26).

For alphabet-modification questions ('first half reversed…'), physically write the 26-letter new sequence and count — never trust mental shifting.

formulas.name: Position from the right
formulas.note: The two positions of the same letter add to 27.

formulas.name: Shifted position
formulas.note: Move right (+) or left (−) by k letters, clamped to 1–26.

tricks.title: EJOTY + tiny shift
tricks.body: Anchor at the nearest of E, J, O, T, Y and step. Position 18: T(20) − 2 = **R**. Two seconds, no counting.

example.q:
**Q.** Which letter is 7th to the right of the 10th letter of the alphabet?

**Sol.** 10th = J; 7 right → 17 = **Q** (J at 10, O at 15, Q at 17).
example.solution: EJOTY converts every position into a ±few-step walk from an anchor.

mistakes: Using 26 instead of 27 in from-the-right conversions.
Slipping past A or Z on shifts — check bounds.
Confusing 'letter at position 10' with '10 letters after it'.
subtopics.notes:
### Positions, mirrors and letter arithmetic

These questions treat the alphabet as a numbered strip of 26 tiles and ask who stands where. Three tools cover everything.

**Tool 1 — absolute positions (EJOTY).** Memorise five anchors: **E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25**. Every other position is a small step from an anchor: G = J − 3 = 7; R = T − 2 = 18; W = Y + 2 = 23. With anchors, "which is the 15th letter" is instant (O), and "how many letters between G and S" is 19 − 7 − 1 = 11 (subtract positions, minus one — the letters *between* exclude both ends).

**Tool 2 — the mirror (from the right).** The letter that is k-th from the **right** stands at position $27 - k$ from the left (and vice versa: position p from the left is $27 - p$ from the right). So the 9th from the right = $27 - 9 = 18$th from the left = R; and T (20th from left) is $27 - 20 = 7$th from the right. The number 27 is the whole trick: 26 letters plus one.

**Tool 3 — letter arithmetic.** "4th to the right of the 12th from the left": convert every clause to a from-the-left position, then add or subtract on the strip. From-the-left + right-steps = add; left-steps = subtract. When a clause says "from the right", convert first ($27-k$), then do the arithmetic:
- 4th right of 12th from left → $12 + 4 = 16$ → P.
- 6th left of 8th from right → $27 - 8 = 19$, then $19 - 6 = 13$ → M.

Watch the two directions: 'to the right of' adds toward Z; 'to the left of' subtracts toward A — because the strip is drawn left = A … right = Z.

**Tool 4 — modified alphabets.** Variants rewrite the strip first, then ask a position:
- *Full reverse:* Z first … A last; position p in the reverse strip = letter $27 - p$ of the normal strip.
- *Half reverse:* first half A-M written backwards, second half normal (or Z-N backwards). Write the new 26-letter strip once, then answer by counting — never by juggling formulas.

**Check every answer by touch.** Confirm with anchors: position 16 must be near T (20) — 4 steps before T is P ✓. If your letter lands more than 5 away from the predicted anchor, recount; that five-second habit catches nearly every off-by-one.

### Quick revision
- EJOTY anchors: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25; step from them, never from A.
- Between G and S: $19-7-1=11$; 'between' excludes both ends.
- Mirror: k-th from right $= 27-k$ from left (and the reverse).
- Multi-clause: convert everything to from-the-left, then add (right) or subtract (left).
- Modified strip: write it out once, then count on paper.

**Off-by-one defence.** Every wrong answer in this subtopic is off by exactly one step: counting the end letter in 'between', forgetting the +1 in the mirror (27, not 26), or stepping the wrong way after 'to the left of'. Anchor-verify the final letter (it must sit within 5 of the predicted anchor) and both errors disappear.

patterns.name: Absolute position via EJOTY anchors
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is the 15th letter' or 'how many letters between X and Y'.
patterns.logic:
1. Step from the nearest anchor (E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25).
2. Between A and B: $|posA - posB| - 1$ ('between' excludes both ends).
3. Confirm the letter sits within 5 of the predicted anchor.

*Why it works:* five anchors turn 26 positions into five short hops.

example.q: **How many letters of the alphabet are there between G and S?**

patterns.name: Mirror positions from the right
patterns.howToSpot: 'k-th from the right' or 'position of letter X from the right'.
patterns.logic:
1. From-right position = $27 - $ from-left position (and the reverse).
2. Convert to from-left, answer with anchors, convert back if asked.
3. Remember the 27: 26 letters + 1.

*Why it works:* the mirror maps the strip onto itself around the midpoint.

example.q: **What is the position of the letter T from the right of the alphabet?**
example.solution: $27 - 20$ = **7th** from the right.

patterns.name: Letter arithmetic (left/right of a position)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which letter is 4th to the right of the 12th from the left' — two clauses in one question.
patterns.logic:
1. Convert every clause to a from-the-left number (mirror any 'from the right').
2. Right-steps add, left-steps subtract.
3. Read the letter off the EJOTY anchors.

*Why it works:* the alphabet strip is a number line in disguise.

example.q: **Which letter is 6th to the left of the 8th letter from the right?**

patterns.name: Modified or reversed alphabet
patterns.howToSpot: 'First half written in reverse', 'alphabet in reverse order', then a position question.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the new 26-letter strip once on paper.
2. Count the asked position on the new strip directly.
3. For the full reverse only: reverse position p = normal letter $27 - p$.

*Why it works:* a rewrite is a one-time setup; after that it is plain counting.

example.q: **If the first half of the alphabet (A-M) is written in reverse order followed by N-Z, which letter is 10th from the left?**
example.solution: New strip: M L K J I H G F E D C B A N O ... → 10th = **D**.

subtopics.title: Dictionary rank and word surgery
subtopics.concept:
Two specialist questions:

1. **Rank of a word** (e.g. the dictionary rank of MACHINE among arrangements of its letters): step letter by letter. At each step count how many *unused* letters are smaller than the current letter — multiply that count by (remaining letters − 1)! and add. Add 1 at the end. This is 'how many words start with earlier letters' accumulation.
2. **Letter surgery**: rearranging a word's letters alphabetically, counting letters that keep their place, or rebuilding words from selected positions — always write the derived sequence out.

The formula as written assumes all letters are **distinct** (every SSC rank question so far uses distinct letters). With repeated letters each block count must also be divided by the factorials of the repeats among the remaining letters.

formulas.name: Rank of a word
formulas.note: At each letter: c_i = unused letters smaller than it, r_i = letters remaining after it.

tricks.title: Count smaller unused letters
tricks.body: Freeze the sorted letter list, and for each letter of the word (left to right) ask: how many still-unused letters are SMALLER? Multiply by the factorial of what remains, sum, +1.

example.q:
**Q.** Rank of CAB among ABC arrangements?

**Sol.** C: A,B smaller → 2×2! = 4. A: none smaller → 0. B: none → 0. Rank = 4 + 0 + 0 + 1 = **5**.
example.solution: Per-letter contribution = smaller-unused × (remaining)!.

mistakes: Forgetting the final +1 (the word itself is not counted by the sums).
Using the original remaining count instead of the shrinking one.
Rearranging letters alphabetically but comparing with the original word wrongly.
subtopics.notes:
### Rank of a word, and other letter-bag questions

Two families live here. Both are procedures — learn the steps once and every instance falls.

**Family 1 — dictionary rank of a word.** "The letters of PRIME are arranged in all possible ways as in a dictionary; what is the rank of PRIME?" The rank counts how many arrangements come **before** the word, plus one. Procedure:
1. Write the word's letters in alphabetical order (E, I, M, P, R for PRIME).
2. Scan the word left to right. At each position, count how many *unused* letters are **smaller** than the current letter. Each smaller letter would start a block of arrangements: add (count) × (arrangements of the remaining letters).
3. 'Arrangements of the remaining letters' = factorial of how many letters are left — divided by the factorials of any repeated-letter counts (a word with two E's has half as many distinct arrangements).
4. Fix the current letter as used and move right. The final total + 1 is the rank.

Example skeleton for PRIME: P is 4th smallest of {E,I,M,P,R} → 3 × 4! before it; then R is 4th of {E,I,M,R} → 3 × 3!; then I is 2nd of {E,I,M} → 1 × 2!; then M is 2nd of {E,M} → 1 × 1!; E is 1st → 0. Rank = 72 + 18 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 94.

**Family 2 — alphabetised spellings.** "If the letters of TABLE are rearranged in alphabetical order, how many letters keep their position?" Write the word, write its letters sorted (A B E L T), and compare column by column. Only exact matches count. TABLE: only L (position 4) matches → one letter.

**Family 3 — form the word from the letters.** "Which word can be formed from the letters of CONVERSATION?" Check each option letter by letter against the bag: cross off a bag letter for every use. Two details decide these: **repeats** (the bag has two O's and two N's — using three O's fails) and **missing letters** (one absent letter kills the option). Scan for the rarest letter in each option first; that fails or passes fastest.

**Family 4 — neighbours in the arrangement list.** "All arrangements of BAT in dictionary order — which is 4th?" The list is short: write it out (ABT, ATB, BAT, BTA, TAB, TBA) and count. For 3 distinct letters the whole list is 6 words; writing it beats any formula.

### Quick revision
- Rank = count smaller-letter blocks position by position + 1; divide by repeat factorials.
- Alphabetise-and-compare: only exact same-position letters count.
- Word-formation: cross off bag letters; watch double letters and one missing letter.
- 3-letter words: write all 6 arrangements and count slots.
- Sanity: the rank must not exceed n! (7! = 5040 for a 7-letter word).

patterns.name: Dictionary rank of a word
patterns.howToSpot: 'All arrangements listed as in a dictionary — what is the rank of the word?'
patterns.logic:
1. Sort the letters alphabetically; scan the word left to right.
2. At each position add (unused letters smaller than the current one) × (arrangements of the rest).
3. Arrangements of the rest = factorial of the count, divided by repeat factorials.
4. Fix the letter, move right; total + 1 = rank.

*Why it works:* each smaller unused letter heads a full block of arrangements that come first.

example.q: **Find the dictionary rank of the word CAB.**
example.solution: C: A and B smaller → 2 × 2! = 4. A fixed; B: nothing smaller. Rank = 4 + 1 = **5** (ABT-style list: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB).

patterns.name: Same-position count after alphabetising
patterns.howToSpot: 'Letters rearranged in alphabetical order — how many letters occupy their original position?'
patterns.logic:
1. Write the word; write its letters sorted beneath it.
2. Compare column by column; count exact matches only.
3. Answer as a number word if the options say so.

*Why it works:* a position survives only if the sorted letter equals the original letter there.

example.q: **If the letters of DERAIL are rearranged in alphabetical order, how many letters remain in their original position?**
example.solution: DERAIL vs ADEILR: D≠A, E≠D, R≠E, A≠I, I≠L, L≠R → **None**.

patterns.name: Forming words from a letter bag
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which word can/cannot be formed from the letters of X?'
patterns.logic:
1. List the bag with repeat counts.
2. For each option, check its rarest letter first; cross off bag letters as used.
3. One missing letter, or one letter needed more often than it appears, kills the option.

*Why it works:* forming a word is a multiset check — counts matter as much as presence.

example.q: **Which word CANNOT be formed from the letters of DISTRIBUTION?**
example.solution: Bag has D,I,S,T,R,B,U,O,N (I×2, T×2). STUDIO ✓, BIRD ✓, ROBUST ✓, BRUSH needs **H** → cannot be formed.

patterns.name: Neighbours in a short arrangement list
patterns.howToSpot: 3-letter words: 'which is the 4th arrangement' or 'what comes just after X' in dictionary order.
patterns.logic:
1. List all 3! = 6 arrangements in dictionary order (a few seconds of writing).
2. Count to the asked slot, or read the requested neighbour.

*Why it works:* for six items, writing the list is faster and safer than any formula.

example.q: **All arrangements of FAN are listed in dictionary order. Which word comes immediately after AFN?**
example.solution: List: AFN, ANF, FAN, FNA, NAF, NFA → after AFN = **ANF**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Words with a shared opening; 'which comes first/last/third'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Compare to the first differing letter; earlier letter wins; prefix sorts before extensions; sort once, number, read.

example.q: **Arrange Scant, Scan, Scandal. Which comes last?**
example.solution: Scan (prefix) → Scandal (5th d) → Scant (5th t) → last = **Scant**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Slot picking in a 4-6 word sort
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A list of near-identical words plus 'which is the Nth'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Strip the stem, sort tails letter by letter, number the list, read the slot; convert 'from the right' to N+1−k.

example.q: **Arrange Statue, Status, Station, Statute, Stature. Which is third from the left?**
example.solution: Station, Statue, Stature, Status, Statute → third = **Stature**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Nth letter', 'k-th from the right', 'letters between X and Y'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchors E=5 J=10 O=15 T=20 Y=25; between = difference − 1; mirror = 27 − position.

example.q: **Which letter is 9th from the right of the English alphabet?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Half the alphabet reversed' plus a position lookup.
pyqPatterns.approach: Write the new strip once, then count on paper; full reverse: position p ↔ letter 27−p.

example.q: **Alphabet reversed (Z first). Which letter is 5th from the left?**
example.solution: Z Y X W V → 5th = **V**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Rank of the word among all arrangements of its letters'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Position by position: smaller unused letters × arrangements of the rest; add, then +1; divide by repeat factorials.

example.q: **Rank of BEAD among all arrangements of its letters?**
example.solution: B: A smaller → 1 × 3! = 6. E: A and D smaller → 2 × 2! = 4. A: nothing smaller. Rank = 6 + 4 + 0 + 1 = **11**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which word can/cannot be formed from the letters of X?'
pyqPatterns.approach: Bag with repeat counts; check each option's rarest letter first; a missing letter or an over-used repeated letter kills the option.

example.q: **Which word CANNOT be formed from the letters of DISTRIBUTION: STUDIO, BIRD, ROBUST, BRUSH?**
example.solution: The bag has no **H** → BRUSH cannot be formed; the rest fit inside the letter counts.

solvedExamples.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Cable, Cabin, Cabaret, Cabbage.** Which word comes **second**?
solvedExamples.solution: All share CAB. 4th letters: A (Cabaret), B (Cabbage), I (Cabin), L (Cable). Order: Cabaret, Cabbage, Cabin, Cable → second = **Cabbage**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: First split point: the 4th letter decides everything here.

solvedExamples.q: Which letter is **6th to the right of the 14th letter** from the left of the English alphabet?
If the letters of the word **WORD** are arranged in all possible ways, what is the **dictionary rank** of the word WORD itself?
solvedExamples.solution: Sorted letters: D, O, R, W. W: 3 smaller → 3×3! = 18. O: 1 smaller left (D) → 1×2! = 2. R: 1 smaller left (D) → 1×1! = 1. D: 0. Rank = 18+2+1+0+1 = **22**.

solvedExamples.q: How many letters are there in the English alphabet **between J and V**?

practice.q: How many letters of the English alphabet are there **between D and P** (not counting D and P)?
practice.shortcut: Positions differ by 12; strictly-between is one less.

practice.q: What is the position of the letter **W from the right** of the English alphabet?
practice.solution: W = 23 from the left → 27 − 23 = **4th** from the right (Z 1st, Y 2nd, X 3rd, W 4th).
practice.shortcut: From-right position = 27 − from-left position.

practice.q: Which letter is **5th to the left of the 20th letter from the right** of the English alphabet?
practice.solution: 20th from the right = 27 − 20 = 7th from the left = G. Five to the left: 7 − 5 = 2 = **B**.
practice.shortcut: Convert from-right to from-left, then shift left.

practice.q: If the **first half of the English alphabet is written in reverse order** (so the sequence begins M, L, K, …) and the rest kept as usual, which letter is **7th to the left of the letter that is 10th from the right** in this new sequence?
practice.solution: New sequence: M L K J I H G F E D C B A N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z. 10th from the right = position 27 − 10 = 17 = Q (the second half is unchanged). Seven to its left = position 10 = **D** (M1 L2 K3 J4 I5 H6 G7 F8 E9 D10).
practice.shortcut: Write the full 26-letter line once; all counting happens on paper.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Nation, Native, Nature, Nautical, Naughty.** Which word comes **third**?
practice.solution: All share NA; the 3rd letter splits them: T-group (Nation, Native, Nature) before U-group (Naughty, Nautical) since T < U. Inside NAT: NATI (Nation, Native) before NATU (Nature); NATIO < NATIV. Order: Nation, Native, Nature, Naughty, Nautical → third = **Nature**.
practice.shortcut: Group by the first split letter: NAT < NAU, then I < U.

practice.q: Which word would come **last** in the dictionary: **Borrow, Border, Borne, Bore, Borough**?
practice.solution: Common prefix BOR. 4th letters: D (Border), E (Bore), N (Borne), O (Borough), R (Borrow). D < E < N < O < R → order: Border, Bore, Borne, Borough, Borrow. Last = **Borrow**.
practice.shortcut: Split at BOR + 4th letter: D E N O R.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Signal, Sight, Silly, Sign, Silent.** Which word is **exactly in the middle**?
practice.solution: SIG group: 4th letter H (Sight) before N (Sign, Signal); Sign is a prefix of Signal → Sign first. SIL group: 4th letter E (Silent) before L (Silly). Full order: Sight, Sign, Signal, Silent, Silly → middle (3rd) = **Signal**.
practice.shortcut: Two prefix-clusters: SIG and SIL; settle each, then splice.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Angel, Angle, Anger, Amble, Amber.** Which word comes **fourth**?
practice.solution: AM group first (Amber, Amble; B < L), then the ANG group at the 4th letter: Angel (E) and Anger (E) precede Angle (L). Angel vs Anger splits at the 5th: L < R. Order: Amber, Amble, Angel, Anger, Angle → fourth = **Anger**.
practice.shortcut: First-letter split (AM/AN), then compare at the first difference only.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Scant, Scan, Scandal.** Which word comes **second**?
practice.solution: SCANDAL vs SCANT: at the 5th letter D < T, so Scandal precedes Scant, and Scan (a prefix) precedes both. Order: Scan, Scandal, Scant → second = **Scandal**.
practice.shortcut: Prefix rule puts SCAN first; then D vs T decides the rest — never compare by length.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Song, Son, Sonar, Sone, Soon.** Which word comes **fourth**?
practice.solution: SON is a prefix of Sonar → Son first. Among SON- words compare the 4th letter: SONA (Sonar) < SONE (Sone) < SONG (Song). SOON splits at the 3rd letter (O > N), so it is last. Order: Son, Sonar, Sone, Song, Soon → fourth = **Song**.
practice.shortcut: Prefix first, then the 4th letter A < E < G; SOO- after all SON-.

practice.q: If the letters of the word **MACHINE** are arranged in all possible ways and the arrangements are listed as in a dictionary, what is the **rank of the word MACHINE**?
practice.solution: Sorted letters: A, C, E, H, I, M, N. Letter-by-letter 'smaller-unused × remaining!': M → 5×6! = 3600; A → 0; C → 0; H → 1×3! = 6 (only E is smaller-unused); I → 1×2! = 2 (E again); N → 1×1! = 1 (E); E → 0. Sum 3600+6+2+1, plus 1 for the word itself = **3610**.
practice.shortcut: Smaller-unused × remaining! per letter, then +1.

practice.q: If the letters of the word **PLANET** are rearranged in alphabetical order, how many letters will remain in the **same position** as in the original word?
practice.solution: Original: P L A N E T. Alphabetical: A E L N P T. Slot by slot: P/A ✗, L/E ✗, A/L ✗, N/N ✓, E/P ✗, T/T ✓ → **two** letters (N and T) stay put.
practice.shortcut: Write both versions one above the other and tick matches.

practice.q: All arrangements of the letters of **BEAD** are listed as in a dictionary. What is the **position of BEAD** in that list?
practice.solution: Sorted letters: A, B, D, E. B → 1 smaller (A) × 3! = 6. E → unused {A, D, E}: 2 smaller × 2! = 4. A → 0. D → 0. Rank = 6 + 4 + 0 + 0 + 1 = **11**.
practice.shortcut: Smaller-unused × remaining! per letter, then +1.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Precise, Preach, Predict, Precede, Precious.** Which word comes **fourth**?
practice.solution: All start PRE. 4th letter: A (Preach) < C (Precede, Precious, Precise) < D (Predict). Inside PREC: 5th letter E (Precede) < I (Precious, Precise); PRECI-O < PRECI-S. Order: Preach, Precede, Precious, Precise, Predict → fourth = **Precise**.
practice.shortcut: Peel the shared prefix one column at a time: PRE → A/C/D → E/I → O/S.

practice.q: Which letter lies **exactly midway between E and U** in the English alphabet?
practice.solution: E = 5, U = 21. Midpoint = (5 + 21) ÷ 2 = 13 → **M**. (Check: 7 letters F–L on one side, 7 letters N–T on the other.)
practice.shortcut: Average the two positions; EJOTY gives 13 = O − 2 = M.

practice.q: Which word comes **first** in the dictionary?
practice.solution: All share MAR. 4th letters: b (Marble), k (Market), g (Margin). b is earliest → **Marble** comes first.
practice.shortcut: Ignore the shared part; only the first differing letter votes.

practice.q: Which word comes **last** in the dictionary?
practice.solution: All share PAN. 4th letters: d (Panda), e (Panel), o (Panorama), t (Pants). t is the latest → **Pants** comes last.
practice.shortcut: The biggest deciding letter wins the last slot.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Sand, Sandwich, Sandy, Sandal.** Which comes **first**?
practice.solution: Sand is a prefix of the other three, and a prefix always sorts **before** its extensions → **Sand** first.
practice.shortcut: Bare stem beats every extension of itself.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Car, Cart, Carton, Cargo.** Which comes **last**?
practice.solution: Car is the prefix of the rest → Car first. Extensions by 4th letter: g (Cargo) vs t (Cart, Carton) → g < t, so Cargo precedes both. Cart is the prefix of Carton → Cart, then Carton. Full order: Car, Cargo, Cart, Carton → last = **Carton**.
practice.shortcut: Prefix first; then the deepest letter decides the end of the list.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Sure, Surge, Surgeon, Surreal, Surplus.** Which comes **third**?
practice.solution: All share SUR. 4th letters: e (Sure), g (Surge, Surgeon), p (Surplus), r (Surreal); e < g < p < r. Inside the g-pair, Surge is the prefix of Surgeon → Surge first. Full order: Sure, Surge, Surgeon, Surplus, Surreal → third = **Surgeon**.
practice.shortcut: Sort the 4th letters e < g < p < r; the prefix splits the g-pair.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Kite, Kind, Kill, Kingdom.** Which comes **second**?
practice.solution: All share KI. 3rd letters: l (Kill), n (Kind, Kingdom), t (Kite); l < n < t. Inside the n-pair, Kind is the prefix of Kingdom → Kind first. Full order: Kill, Kind, Kingdom, Kite → second = **Kind**.
practice.shortcut: Sort the 3rd letters l < n < t; the prefix splits the n-pair.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Melon, Melody, Mellow, Member.** Which pair sits on **adjacent** slots?
practice.solution: 4th letters: o (Melon), o (Melody), l (Mellow), b (Member) → Member, Mellow, then Melody (5th d) before Melon (5th n). Order: Member, Mellow, Melody, Melon → the last two are adjacent: **Melon and Melody**.
practice.shortcut: Write the numbered order; adjacency is just slots differing by one.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Freeze, Fridge, Friend, Fright.** Which comes **second**?
practice.solution: FR common. 3rd letters: e (Freeze) vs i (the rest) → Freeze first. The i-group: 4th letters d (Fridge), e (Friend), g (Fright) → Fridge, Friend, Fright. Second = **Fridge**.
practice.shortcut: First split at the 3rd letter, then sort the bigger group by the 4th.

practice.q: Which word would a dictionary list **first**: Play, Player or Plays?
practice.solution: Play is a prefix of both Player and Plays, so it sorts before them → **Play** first.
practice.shortcut: Prefix beats extensions — no deeper comparison needed.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Regal, Region, Regime, Register, Regret.** Which comes **last**?
practice.solution: All share REG. 4th letters: a (Regal), i (Regime, Region, Register), r (Regret); a < i < r, so Regal first and Regret **last** — no 5th letter can rescue Register because its 4th letter (i) already loses to r. Order: Regal, Regime, Region, Register, Regret → last = **Regret**.
practice.shortcut: The 4th-letter sort (a < i < r) already fixes both ends of this list.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Honest, Honey, Hong, Honk, Honour.** Which word is exactly in the **middle**?
practice.solution: All share HON. 4th letters: e (Honest, Honey), g (Hong), k (Honk), o (Honour); e < g < k < o. The e-pair: 5th letters e (Honest) vs y (Honey) → Honest first. Full order: Honest, Honey, Hong, Honk, Honour → middle (slot 3 of 5) = **Hong**.
practice.shortcut: Order the 4th letters e < g < k < o; slot 3 of five is the middle.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Chalk, Charm, Chart, Chase, Chatter.** Which is the **fourth** word?
practice.solution: All share CHA. 4th letters: l (Chalk), r (Charm, Chart), s (Chase), t (Chatter); l < r < s < t. The r-pair: 5th letters m (Charm) vs t (Chart) → Charm first. Full order: Chalk, Charm, Chart, Chase, Chatter → fourth = **Chase**.
practice.shortcut: Sort the 4th letters; only the r-pair needs one more letter.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Colonel, Colony, Column, Colour, Colossus.** Which word comes **just after Colony**?
practice.solution: All share COL. 4th letters: o (Colonel, Colony, Colour, Colossus) vs u (Column) → the o-group first. 5th letters: n (Colonel, Colony), s (Colossus), u (Colour); n < s < u. The n-pair: 6th letters e (Colonel) vs y (Colony) → Colonel, Colony. Full order: Colonel, Colony, Colossus, Colour, Column → just after Colony = **Colossus**.
practice.shortcut: u sends Column last; inside the o-group sort 5th letters n < s < u.

practice.q: Which word comes **last** in the dictionary: **Panther, Pant, Pantomime, Pantry**?
practice.solution: Pant is the prefix of all → first. 5th letters of the rest: h (Panther), o (Pantomime), r (Pantry); h < o < r. Order: Pant, Panther, Pantomime, Pantry → last = **Pantry**.
practice.shortcut: Prefix first; then h < o < r lines up the rest.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Judge, Judo, Joust, Journal, Jostle.** Which word is **second from the right**?
practice.solution: 2nd letters: o (Jostle, Journal, Joust) vs u (Judge, Judo); o < u → the o-group comes first. 3rd letters: s (Jostle) vs u (Journal, Joust) → Jostle first. 4th letters: r (Journal) vs s (Joust) → Journal, Joust. Full order: Jostle, Journal, Joust, Judge, Judo → slot 5 + 1 − 2 = 4 → **Judge**.
practice.shortcut: The 2nd letter splits J-o... before J-u... — check column two before assuming a shared stem.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Decamp, Decay, Deceive, Decent, December.** Which word comes **immediately before Deceive**?
practice.solution: All share DEC. 4th letters: a (Decamp, Decay), e (the rest) → the a-pair first: 5th letters m (Decamp) vs y (Decay) → Decamp, Decay. The e-group by 5th letters: i (Deceive), m (December), n (Decent). Full order: Decamp, Decay, Deceive, December, Decent → before Deceive = **Decay**.
practice.shortcut: Sort the 4th letters a < e; the a-pair hides Decamp vs Decay at the 5th letter.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Statue, Status, Station, Statute, Stature.** Which is **third from the left**?
practice.solution: All share STAT. 5th letters: i (Station) vs u (the rest) → Station first. The u-group by 6th letters: e (Statue), r (Stature), s (Status), t (Statute); e < r < s < t. Full order: Station, Statue, Stature, Status, Statute → third = **Stature**.
practice.shortcut: Compare position 6: e < r < s < t — Statue, Stature, Status, Statute.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Mystery, Mystic, Myself, Myopia.** Which comes **first**?
practice.solution: MY common. 3rd letters: s (Mystery, Mystic, Myself) vs o (Myopia); o < s → **Myopia** first, whatever happens later. (Full order: Myopia, Myself, Mystery, Mystic.)
practice.shortcut: The earliest 3rd letter ends the contest at once — check the o-word first.

practice.q: Which is the **15th letter** of the English alphabet?
practice.solution: EJOTY anchor: O = 15. The 15th letter is **O**.
practice.shortcut: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25 — read anchors, never count from A.

practice.q: How many letters of the English alphabet are there **between G and S**?
practice.solution: pos S = 19, pos G = 7. Letters between = 19 − 7 − 1 = **11** ('between' excludes both ends).
practice.shortcut: Difference of positions minus one.

practice.q: Which letter is **9th from the right** of the English alphabet?
practice.solution: k-th from the right = position 27 − k from the left: 27 − 9 = 18 → **R**.
practice.shortcut: Mirror number 27: from-right k ↔ from-left 27−k.

practice.q: What is the position of the letter **T from the right** of the English alphabet?
practice.solution: T is 20th from the left (EJOTY anchor T=20). Mirror: 27 − 20 = **7th** from the right.
practice.shortcut: Anchor first, then 27 − position.

practice.q: Which letter is **4th to the right of the 12th letter from the left**?
practice.solution: 12th letter = L; 4 steps right: 12 + 4 = 16 → **P**.
practice.shortcut: Convert to numbers, add right-steps, read off T=20 anchor (16 = T − 4).

practice.q: Which letter is **6th to the left of the 8th letter from the right**?
practice.solution: 8th from the right = 27 − 8 = 19 (S). 6 steps left: 19 − 6 = 13 → **M**.
practice.shortcut: Mirror first (27−8), then subtract the left-steps.

practice.q: The first half of the alphabet (A-M) is written in **reverse order**, followed by N-Z. Which letter is **10th from the left** of the new arrangement?
practice.solution: New strip: M L K J I H G F E D C B A N O P ... Count to 10: M(1) L(2) K(3) J(4) I(5) H(6) G(7) F(8) E(9) D(10) → **D**.
practice.shortcut: Write the new strip once; then it is plain counting.

practice.q: The alphabet is written as A to M, followed by **Z to N in reverse**. Which letter is **20th from the left** of this arrangement?
practice.solution: New strip positions 1-13: A-M; positions 14-26: Z, Y, X, W, V, U, T, S ... 20th = 14 + 6 → count from Z: Z(14) Y(15) X(16) W(17) V(18) U(19) T(20) → **T**.
practice.shortcut: Position 20 sits 6 steps into the reversed half starting at Z (position 14).

practice.q: All arrangements of the letters of **CAB** are listed as in a dictionary. What is the **rank of CAB**?
practice.solution: Letters sorted: A, B, C. Position 1 (C): A and B are smaller → 2 × 2! = 4 arrangements come first. Positions 2-3 (A, B): nothing smaller. Rank = 4 + 1 = **5** (list: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB).
practice.shortcut: Small words: write the 6-item list and count — same answer, zero algebra.

practice.q: The letters of **MONSTER** are arranged in all possible ways as in a dictionary. What is the **rank of MONSTER**?
practice.solution: Sorted letters: E, M, N, O, R, S, T. M: E smaller → 1 × 6! = 720. O (left M,E,N): E, N smaller → 2 × 4! = 48. N (left E): 1 × 3! = 6. S (left O,R): O, R smaller → 2 × 2! = 4. T (left R): 1 × 1! = 1. E: 0. Rank = 720 + 48 + 6 + 4 + 1 + 1 = **1001**.
practice.shortcut: Track the unused set after each fix; multiply the smaller-letter count by the remaining factorial.

practice.q: If the letters of **PRIME** are arranged in all possible ways as in a dictionary, what is the **rank of PRIME**?
practice.solution: Sorted letters: E, I, M, P, R. P: E, I, M smaller → 3 × 4! = 72. R (left E, I, M): 3 smaller → 3 × 3! = 18. I (left E, M): 1 smaller → 1 × 2! = 2. M (left E): 1 × 1! = 1. E: 0. Rank = 72 + 18 + 2 + 1 + 1 = **94**.
practice.shortcut: 720-then-720 style: the first letter usually contributes the bulk.

practice.q: If the letters of **TABLE** are rearranged in alphabetical order, how many letters **keep their original position**?
practice.solution: TABLE vs its sorted form ABE L T: T-A-B-L-E under A-B-E-L-T → only L sits at position 4 in both → **one** letter.
practice.shortcut: Write one word under the other; count exact column matches only.

practice.q: If the letters of **SIGNED** are rearranged in alphabetical order, how many letters **keep their original position**?
practice.solution: SIGNED vs its sorted form D-E-G-I-N-S → only G (position 3) matches → **one** letter.
practice.shortcut: Compare columns; one match is the usual exam answer — verify, don't assume.

practice.q: Which word **can be formed** from the letters of **CONVERSATION**?
practice.solution: Bag: C, O×2, N×2, V, E, R, S, A, T, I. CREATION needs C, R, E, A, T, I, O, N — all present, no letter used twice. CARPENTER needs P (absent); TRANSPIRE needs P (absent); CONSUMER needs U and M (absent) → **CREATION**.
practice.shortcut: Hunt the rarest letter of each option first; P/U fail three options instantly.

practice.q: Which word **cannot be formed** from the letters of **DISTRIBUTION**?
practice.solution: Bag: D, I×2, S, T×2, R, B, U, O, N. BRUSH needs **H**, which is not in the word → cannot be formed. STUDIO, BIRD and ROBUST use only available letters within their counts.
practice.shortcut: One missing letter is enough — scan for absent letters first.

practice.q: All arrangements of the letters of **BAT** are listed in dictionary order. Which is the **4th** word?
practice.solution: Write the six: ABT, ATB, BAT, BTA, TAB, TBA. The 4th is **BTA**.
practice.shortcut: Six arrangements, five seconds — write them out, no formula needed.

practice.q: All arrangements of **FAN** are listed in dictionary order. Which word comes **immediately after AFN**?
practice.solution: The list: AFN, ANF, FAN, FNA, NAF, NFA. After AFN = **ANF**.
practice.shortcut: Same first letter → the deeper letter decides the neighbour.

practice.q: Arrange as in a dictionary: **Silver, Silk, Sinful, Single.** Which word is **second from the right**?
practice.solution: All share SI. 3rd letters: l (Silk, Silver) vs n (Sinful, Single); l < n. The l-pair: 4th k (Silk) vs v (Silver) → Silk, Silver. The n-pair: 4th f (Sinful) vs g (Single) → Sinful, Single. Full order: Silk, Silver, Sinful, Single → slot 4 + 1 − 2 = 3 → **Sinful**.
practice.shortcut: Sort the 3rd letters l < n; then slot N+1−k for the right-count.
